passage:
Manager's note, Friday. Ritu writes: Over three weeks I watched how news moves on our floor. The reorganisation was known at the pantry two days before I announced it. Divya from accounts had it first and was passing it along with a knowing look. Saurabh, who joined last month and eats at his desk, heard it from the tea vendor and then asked me quietly, “Is my role safe?” He looked tired, as if he had carried that question for two days. Others around the printer talked freely.

What I did next: I called a short team meeting at 4 p.m. the same day, shared what I knew and what I didn't, and told Saurabh directly that his role was unchanged. I'll send updates each Friday so nobody depends on the pantry.

qa.q: How many days before the announcement did the pantry know about the reorganisation?
qa.a: The pantry knew two days before Ritu announced it.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's quiet question, “Is my role safe?”, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Saurabh had worried for two days, feeling outside the circle and unsure, and waited to ask.

qa.q: What did Ritu decide to do to reduce dependence on the pantry?
qa.a: Ritu called a team meeting the same day and promised updates each Friday.

qa.q: What might it be like for Saurabh, who joined last month, to hear things last?
qa.a: Saurabh may feel anxious and excluded, always the last to know while others hold the power of early news.

grounding: A manager's note shows news travelling through the pantry before official announcements, with a recent joiner outside the grapevine feeling anxious.

passage:
Thursday, 11 p.m. Minakshi knew about the reshuffle before HR did. Again. She stands at the pantry with her coffee and people drift over like she's a small radio. Today three people went silent when I walked past, then started again. I heard “Vikas is moving to another city” before anyone told me my own team was changing. My stomach knotted.

Weird thing: Minakshi isn't unkind. When Kabir asked her something, she said, “I'm not sure that's true.” I think she likes being the person who knows. I might like it too. I just don't want to be the one waiting for crumbs.

Note to self: ask the manager directly tomorrow.
— Rehana

qa.q: What did Rehana hear before anyone said the team was changing?
qa.a: Rehana heard that Vikas is moving to another city before anyone told Rehana about the team changing.

qa.q: Why does Rehana feel a knot in the stomach?
qa.a: Rehana feels shut out and anxious, hearing news about the own team from the pantry before official word.

qa.q: What does Rehana decide to do the next day?
qa.a: Rehana decides to ask the manager directly.

qa.q: What might Minakshi feel about being the person who knows?
qa.a: Minakshi probably enjoys the attention and sense of power, and may feel pressure to keep being first.

grounding: A young professional sees news travel through the pantry before official announcements, feeling anxious while someone with grapevine access holds power.

passage:
At the sugar mill office outside Kolhapur, real news arrived at the tea stall before it reached any notice board. Jeevan, who had worked there two years, always knew first. Which clerk was being transferred, whose promotion was stuck, when bonuses might come.
He liked it. When he walked into the tea stall, people made space for him.
Tanvir, who had joined only three months ago from Solapur, didn't know anyone at the stall. One morning he asked Jeevan, “Is it true they're moving the new clerks to the night shift?”
Jeevan shrugged. “That's what they're saying.”
Tanvir went pale. He had a newborn at home. That whole day, Jeevan watched him check the notice board every hour, and felt less proud of what he knew.

qa.q: Where did the real news arrive first?
qa.a: At the tea stall, before it reached any notice board.

qa.q: How did Jeevan's feelings change watching Tanvir?
qa.a: At first he felt proud and important, but watching Tanvir check the board every hour, he felt uneasy and less proud.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do to help Tanvir?
qa.a: He could admit it's only talk, and suggest Tanvir ask the office manager directly about the shifts.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have felt that day?
qa.a: He was likely anxious and worried, with a newborn at home and only rumours to go on.

grounding: Shows a young clerk who enjoys early access to the office grapevine, while a newcomer outside it feels anxious.

passage:
At the design firm in Osaka, the real news always travelled in the smoking corner and in a group chat of senior staff. Hiroshi was in both. He knew about the reorganisation a week early.
In the office, people treated him differently. Juniors brought him coffee and asked, casually, “Anything new?”
Clara, the only foreign designer on the team, wasn't in the group chat. She didn't smoke. One day she stopped Hiroshi by the printer. “Everyone's whispering. Is my contract safe? Nobody tells me anything.”
Hiroshi saw her hands clutching the pages. He realised she had spent a week worried, while he had enjoyed knowing.
“I honestly don't know about contracts,” he said. “But I'll ask our manager to tell the whole team properly.”

qa.q: Where did the real news travel?
qa.a: In the smoking corner and in a group chat of senior staff.

qa.q: What was Hiroshi feeling when he saw Clara's hands?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, realising she had worried for a week while he enjoyed knowing.

qa.q: Why is asking the manager to tell the whole team a good step?
qa.a: It replaces the grapevine with official facts, so outsiders like Clara don't have to live on rumours.

qa.q: How is Clara affected by being outside the grapevine?
qa.a: She feels anxious and left out, unsure about her contract while others whisper.

grounding: Shows a young professional who enjoys grapevine access, until he sees how anxious a colleague outside it has become.

passage:
By 10 a.m. on Monday, the pantry at the insurance office knew. "The Mumbai team's being merged with ours," said Priyanka, pouring tea, with the small smile of someone who'd heard first. "Three people are moving desks. I know who." Saurabh watched the circle tighten around her.
Vishal, at the next desk, wasn't in the pantry. He'd joined four months ago and wasn't in the unofficial lunch group. By noon he'd heard only half of it, "people moving". He refreshed his email every few minutes and asked Saurabh twice, "Did you hear anything about me?"
The official email from HR came at 5:30. Nobody on their floor was moving. Priyanka shrugged. "Well, it was close." Vishal breathed out as if he'd been holding it all day.
Saurabh decided that next time he heard something in the pantry, he'd ask where it came from before repeating it, and he'd make sure Vishal got invited to lunch.

qa.q: What time did the official email from HR arrive?
What did Saurabh feel watching Vishal refresh his email all day?
qa.a: Saurabh felt uneasy and sympathetic, seeing how the pantry talk left an outsider anxious while insiders felt important.

qa.q: What did Saurabh decide, and how could it help?
qa.a: To ask where news comes from before repeating it and to bring Vishal into lunch, which cuts false rumours and the gap between insiders and outsiders.

qa.q: What was the day like for Vishal?
qa.a: Vishal spent it anxious and on edge, hearing half a rumour and fearing it was about him until 5:30.

grounding: Shows a young professional watching news race through the pantry before any official word, empowering insiders and leaving outsiders anxious.
